analysis.one_liner: Lets EPA require stormwater pollution permits for oil, gas, and mining sites.
analysis.headline: The bill to close a Clean Water Act loophole for oil and gas stormwater runoff was introduced and referred to committee, where it died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The FRESHER Act would have removed a Clean Water Act exemption that currently bars the EPA from requiring water pollution permits for stormwater runoff from oil and gas operations and from certain mining sites. It also directed the Interior Department to study whether runoff from oil and gas operations contaminates groundwater and drinking-water aquifers. The bill never advanced past its introduction and committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near or downstream from oil and gas operations — including fracking sites — and rely on local streams, wells, and aquifers for drinking water. The bill would have let the EPA require permits that set limits on polluted runoff before it reaches waterways, and the required Interior Department study would have given the public and Congress hard data on contamination near drilling sites.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near oil and gas drilling sites

how_it_helps.text: Removes the legal exemption that stops the EPA from requiring Clean Water Act discharge permits for stormwater runoff from oil and gas operations and from mining sites, allowing pollution limits to be set and enforced at those sites.

Directs the Interior Department to study stormwater runoff from oil and gas operations, including measurable contamination, groundwater resources, and how susceptible local aquifers are to contamination, with a report to Congress within a year.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas operators and certain mining operations, which would have had to apply for discharge permits, monitor their runoff, and limit pollution instead of operating under the exemption. Some of those compliance costs could be passed on through energy and mineral prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have added permitting and monitoring costs for oil, gas, and mining operators, and those costs can be significant for smaller operators and may be passed on in energy prices.

The bill itself acknowledges the data gap: it requires a federal study of contamination and aquifer susceptibility rather than acting only on existing evidence, and its scope was limited to stormwater runoff rather than the full range of drilling-related pollution.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — enforceable limits on polluted runoff near drilling and mining sites, plus hard data on aquifer contamination — is real but narrowly targeted at a specific pollution pathway. The cost is added compliance work for operators, which is the kind of burden Clean Water Act permitting routinely imposes on other industries already covered by the law. The tradeoff favored the public, though the bill's narrow scope and the study requirement suggest its sponsors saw the evidence base as incomplete.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up before the Congress ended, so it never got a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Cardin introduced the bill on June 11, 2015, joined by Democratic Senators Merkley, Whitehouse, and Feinstein as original cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the committee did not hold a hearing, report the bill, or schedule a vote, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas operators, who kept the Clean Water Act exemption from stormwater discharge permits, and mining operations, which kept theirs as well.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas operators keeping their permit exemption

for.name: Ben Cardin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought it to the Senate floor for introduction.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Jim Inhofe
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that never scheduled any action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All six Senate supporters — the sponsor and five cosponsors — were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-chaired committee never moved the bill.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers (including fracking operations)
industries.note: The bill's main target: it would have stripped the Clean Water Act exemption that keeps oil and gas sites off the hook for stormwater discharge permits, forcing them to control polluted runoff. That industry interest runs directly against the interest of nearby residents in uncontaminated water.
The bill would also have made mining stormwater runoff subject to EPA discharge permits, ending the same exemption the industry currently enjoys.
